summaries.example: Imagine a school hearing about a broken window. A student saw what happened, a video shows the event, and a ball is found nearby. These may help the decision-maker. But a student’s favorite color probably would not help explain who broke the window. The useful information must connect to the question being decided.
summaries.summary: Legal evidence is not one single thing. It may be testimony from a witness, a document, or a physical object. It may also mean a fact that has been established or a reason for drawing a conclusion about an important issue. Courts usually ask whether proposed evidence is relevant, material, and admissible. Relevant evidence has a connection to a fact. A material fact matters under the law of the case. Admissibility concerns legal rules that permit or exclude certain evidence, even when it seems useful. Hearsay—an out-of-court statement offered to prove that what it says is true—is one example of evidence that is often restricted. At the end, the fact-finder weighs the evidence and decides whether it is strong enough for the required standard of proof. Philosophers and legal scholars disagree about whether evidence should be understood mainly through probability, through explanations of what happened, or through the completeness and testing of the evidence. The entry focuses on the modern Anglo-American legal tradition and notes that legal systems do not all understand evidence in the same way.
key_ideas: In law, “evidence” can mean different things: a statement, a document, an object, or a fact supported by those things.
Evidence must connect to an important question before it can help a court.
Even useful information may be kept out because special legal rules say it should not be used in a certain way.
After evidence is received, the fact-finder must decide how strongly it supports the competing accounts.
summaries.why_it_matters: Courts make important decisions about people’s rights and responsibilities. Clear ideas about evidence can help courts focus on information that bears on the case, avoid unfair reasoning, and explain why some information is accepted while other information is excluded. The topic also shows why deciding what happened is difficult: evidence can be incomplete, and the same fact may support more than one story.

important_terms.definition: Information, an object, or a statement used to help decide whether a claim about what happened is true.
A connection that makes one fact help support or weaken another fact.
A fact that matters under the rules of the case.
A person or group responsible for deciding disputed facts, such as a judge or jury.
A legal rule that allows or blocks evidence from being used in a trial.

questions_to_think_about: Why should a court ignore facts that do not help answer the question in the case?
Can information be useful in everyday life but not allowed in court?
Why might a court want rules about which evidence people may use?
Is one piece of evidence enough to decide what happened?

summaries.example: Suppose a plaintiff claims that a bus company caused an injury. The plaintiff can establish that a bus caused the injury, but cannot identify its company. Evidence that the blue company owns 75% of the town’s buses seems to make liability statistically likely. Yet the source discusses why many lawyers would regard this alone as insufficient: the percentage does not identify the particular bus involved. This illustrates a dispute between mathematical probability and approaches that ask whether the evidence supports a concrete explanation of the event.
summaries.summary: The legal concept of evidence is plural and context-sensitive. In one use, evidence consists of testimony, documents, and physical objects. In another, it is a factual proposition established by such items. In a third, it is a premise from which an inference can be drawn toward a material fact. In a fourth, it means what the law treats as receivable in court. The entry examines the conditions for receiving evidence: relevance, materiality, and admissibility. Relevance is relational rather than intrinsic; a fact is relevant only in relation to a proposition it may support or undermine. Materiality is supplied by the substantive law defining the charge or claim, and a disputed material fact is a fact in issue. Admissibility adds legal restrictions that may exclude evidence despite its logical support, as with some uses of hearsay or character evidence. The entry then turns to evidential strength. Probative value concerns individual items, sufficiency concerns whether the whole body meets the applicable standard of proof, and evidential completeness concerns how substantial the available basis is. Some theories model these matters with likelihood ratios and Bayesian updating. Others object that reference classes, prior probabilities, dependent evidence, and complex calculations make such models difficult to apply. Explanatory or relative-plausibility theories instead compare competing accounts. These approaches also face criticisms, including the risk that apparently coherent narratives conceal bias. The source presents these disagreements without treating any one framework as decisively established.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes at least four uses of “evidence”: sensory objects, established factual propositions, premises for inferences, and what law permits the court to receive.
Receivability is commonly analyzed through relevance, materiality, and admissibility, though legal terminology is not perfectly uniform.
Logical relevance is often treated as a non-legal relation, while some theorists argue that legal relevance requires more than minimal support or is shaped by precedent and legal judgment.
Mathematical models can clarify likelihoods, but reference-class choices and limited data make their application contestable.
The sufficiency of all the evidence is not obviously reducible to a probability threshold; statistical cases can produce intuitively unacceptable results.
Exclusionary rules may protect fairness, reduce misleading reasoning, encourage better evidence, allocate risks of error, or serve other legal purposes, but their value and effects are disputed.
summaries.why_it_matters: Evidence law structures the process by which legal institutions turn contested events into decisions. Its distinctions help separate questions that are often blurred: whether a fact bears on another fact, whether that target fact legally matters, whether a form of proof may be used, and how much support the complete record provides. These distinctions also expose the limits of purely numerical approaches. A probability may be high without identifying the individual responsible, while a persuasive narrative may be vulnerable to selective background assumptions. Studying legal evidence therefore connects law with epistemology, probability, reasoning, fairness, and institutional design.

important_terms.definition: In legal reasoning, something offered to establish a factual claim; the term may refer to objects, facts, inferential premises, or conditions for courtroom use.
A relation in which one fact tends to support or undermine another fact; whether it exists depends on the facts and background knowledge.
A fact that has legal significance because it bears on an element of the claim or charge.
The legal status of evidence that permits it to be presented or used for a particular purpose in court.
A disputed material fact that a party must establish in the case.
The degree to which an item supports or weakens a hypothesis or factual proposition.
The amount or character of support needed before a fact-finder may reach a verdict for the party with the burden of proof.
Reasoning that compares competing accounts and favors the explanation that best fits the available evidence and events.

questions_to_think_about: Should evidence count as relevant whenever it changes a probability, even by a tiny amount?
Does excluding hearsay concern the truth of the statement, or the fairness of relying on a statement that cannot be tested in court?
Why might a high statistical probability fail to justify liability in an individual case?
Should judges use formal probability calculations, competing explanations, or both?
How should a legal system balance accurate fact-finding against fairness and protection from misleading evidence?

summaries.example: A student council is deciding whether a team damaged school equipment. One student saw a team member near the equipment, and another student heard someone say, “Our team did it,” outside the meeting. The first report may be relevant, but it does not prove everything by itself. The second report is hearsay if it is used to prove that the team really did the damage. The council might allow it for another purpose, such as showing that the speaker made the statement. This shows the difference between information being connected to a question and being allowed for a particular use.
summaries.summary: The source explains that legal evidence has several related meanings. It can be a witness’s testimony, a document, or a physical object. It can also be a factual proposition established by those materials, or a premise used to reason toward a fact that matters in the case. Finally, “evidence” can mean what the law permits a court to receive. For something to be receivable, the source highlights relevance, materiality, and admissibility. Relevance is a relationship: a fact must have some bearing on another fact or explanation. Materiality asks whether that target fact matters under the law defining the claim or charge. A disputed material fact is a fact in issue. Admissibility concerns additional legal rules that may exclude relevant evidence or restrict how it may be used. Hearsay is an important example: an out-of-court statement may be useful in ordinary life, but legal systems often limit its use to prove the truth of what was said. The entry also discusses how courts evaluate evidence after receiving it. Probative value concerns an individual item; sufficiency asks whether the full collection reaches the required standard of proof; and evidential completeness concerns how much of the relevant basis is available. One approach uses probability and likelihood ratios. Other approaches stress competing explanations and the way evidence fits into a broader account. The source presents continuing disagreement about how these methods should work and about the purposes served by exclusionary rules.
key_ideas: The word “evidence” can refer to a thing presented in court, a fact established by that thing, a premise for an inference, or information that satisfies legal conditions.
A fact is not relevant all by itself. It is relevant in relation to a question or another fact.
Relevance, materiality, and admissibility are different conditions, although lawyers sometimes use the words loosely.
Some scholars describe relevance with probability, while others emphasize explanations, background knowledge, or the role of the evidence in a larger story.
The strength of evidence includes the support supplied by one item, the sufficiency of the whole collection, and the completeness of what is available.
Evidence rules involve both truth-seeking and concerns such as fairness, prejudice, confusion, cost, and the danger of unreliable reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Legal decisions depend on judgments about disputed facts, but facts are rarely presented perfectly. The concepts in this topic help explain why a court may ask several different questions: Does this information connect to the issue? Does the issue matter legally? May the information be used in this way? How strongly does the complete record support one side? Understanding those questions makes it easier to see why evidence rules are not simply a list of facts that are true or false. They are also rules about reasoning, fairness, and the risks of error.

important_terms.definition: Something used to support a claim about what happened, including testimony, documents, physical objects, or an established fact.
A relationship in which one fact gives some reason to think another fact is true or false.
Importance under the law governing the dispute; a fact is material when it affects the legal claim or charge.
Whether the rules of a legal system allow evidence to be presented or relied on for a specified purpose.
A material fact that is disputed and must be decided in the case.
The strength of a particular item of evidence in supporting a conclusion.
The level of support required for a court to decide for the party that has the burden of proof.
A statement made outside court that is offered to prove that what the statement says is true.

questions_to_think_about: Can a fact be logically relevant but still excluded by a legal rule? Why?
Why does the same piece of evidence sometimes have different strength in different situations?
What is the problem with deciding an individual case only from statistics about a group?
Would you trust a best explanation if it were based on a few untested assumptions?
Why might a court use fixed evidence rules instead of deciding every item freely?
